extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and copyeditors preparing English-language manuscripts (esp. scientific/technical and multilingual texts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines from the Chicago Manual of Style on abbreviations, units of measure, chemical element names, commercial/US measures, and treatment of languages other than English (italics, translations, quotations, transliteration, Unicode). Intended to guide formatting and editorial decisions for manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: SI numeric range and use of prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Only numbers between 0.1 and 1,000 should be used to express the quantity of any SI unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SI prefixes instead of very large or very small numeric values: e.g., 12,000 meters → 12 km (not 12 000 m), 0.003 cubic centimeters → 3 mm (not 0.003 cm3). See also spacing/grouping conventions (9.56).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between numerals and unit symbols (SI usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: A space usually appears between the numeral and any abbreviation or symbol; SI usage also stipulates a space before a percentage sign (%) or before a degree symbol used for temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago notes these SI exceptions but does not require them in its publications. Compare examples for SI vs Chicago style (e.g., percent and degree formatting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derived units: standard names and equivalent forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain derived units have special names and symbols and may be expressed in different equivalent ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the weber may be expressed as Wb or as the volt second (Vs or V·s). Provide consistent usage appropriate to context; table 10.49 lists common derived units (e.g., Hz, V, W).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-SI units accepted within SI contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some widely used units (e.g., liter, metric ton, hour) are not part of SI but are accepted for use within the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize L for liter (to avoid confusion with numeral 1); use standard abbreviations such as L, t (metric ton), h (hour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical coordinates formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Right ascension (RA or α) is given in hours, minutes, and seconds (abbreviations set as superscripts); declination (δ) is given in degrees, minutes, and seconds using degree, prime, and double prime symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 14h 6m 7s  -49° 8' 22". Decimal fractions of basic units are indicated as shown (e.g., 14h6m7s,2  +34°.26). See IAU and Chicago examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical element naming conventions (IUPAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: IUPAC is the recognized body that formally approves element names; element names are always lowercased, and symbols have an initial capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a symbol is based on a term other than the common name (e.g., Sb for stibium), indicate the term in parentheses. Use provisional Latin-based names for undiscovered/unconfirmed elements (e.g., ununoctium) until official naming; arrange element lists alphabetically by common name. Do not use periods with symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional names for undiscovered elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Undiscovered or unconfirmed elements are provisionally assigned Latin-based names reflecting digits of their atomic number (e.g., ununoctium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update when IUPAC confirmation/naming occurs (example: element 118 confirmed in 2015 and named oganesson in 2016).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods in US measure abbreviations: scientific vs nonscientific contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In scientific copy, abbreviations for US units of measure are usually set without periods; in nonscientific contexts, periods are customary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the context: e.g., scientific: 'ft', 'in'; nonscientific: 'ft.' 'in.' See also 10.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural forms of abbreviations of measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations of units of measure are identical in the singular and the plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same abbreviation whether singular or plural (exceptions noted elsewhere). Example: '12 gal.' and '3 pt.'—the abbreviation does not change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronunciation of unit expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit in an expression such as 0.5 yd. or 1.5 yd. is generally pronounced as if it were plural (e.g., 'point five yards'); the singular is reserved for measures of exactly one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading aloud, treat fractional values as plural even if the abbreviation form is unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foot and inch symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper symbols for foot and inch are prime (’) and double prime (”), not single (') and double (”) quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In expressions of height/length like 6 ft., 1 in., display compactly as 6'1" (no space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exponents for area or volume abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exponents are sometimes used with abbreviations to designate area or volume, but only when no ambiguity can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 425 ft. (means 425 square feet not 425 ft. by 425 ft.); 638 ft.3 (= 638 cu. ft.). Use clear notation to avoid misreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight/mass systems and disambiguation
rubrics_metrics.description: The US system comprises three systems of weight and mass: avoirdupois (common), troy (jewelers), and apothecaries’ measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If necessary, refer an abbreviation to the appropriate system (e.g., lb. av., lb. t., lb. ap.) to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for time in nontechnical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Common time abbreviations (sec., h. or hr., mo., min., d. or day, yr.) are used mainly in nontechnical contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In nontechnical writing, plurals of these abbreviations are often formed by adding an s (e.g., 5 secs., 12 hrs., 15 yrs.). Consult technical sections for different practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial abbreviations styling
rubrics_metrics.description: As with many other abbreviations in nonscientific contexts, periods for abbreviations of commercial terms are normally used in lowercased forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conventional abbreviations (acct., amt., ASAP, APR, FY, etc.) and follow Chicago cross-references (10.42–43, 10.64–68). Provide full forms where clarity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize non-English words and phrases not in standard English dictionaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Italics are used for isolated words and phrases from another language, especially if they are not listed in a standard English-language dictionary or are likely to be unfamiliar to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a foreign term becomes familiar through repeated use in a work, italicize only on first occurrence; if rare, italics may be retained. Examples provided (French, German usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization and pluralization of foreign words
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the term appears in a standard English dictionary, observe the capitalization conventions of the original language; form plurals as in the original language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: German nouns retain capitalization (Computer), French adjectives remain lowercase (française); plural of Blumen (not Blumes). Consult language-specific rules (11.18 ff.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting longer passages in another language
rubrics_metrics.description: An entire sentence or a passage of two or more sentences in another language is usually set in roman and, unless set as a block quotation, enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short isolated words/phrases use italics; longer passages remain roman and quoted (or block-quoted). See chapters 13 and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of non-English proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: With the exception of titles of books and the like, proper nouns from other languages are generally not italicized; capitalization should follow predominant usage in the original language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the editor is unfamiliar with the language, consult an expert or the author; when in doubt, opt for sentence-style capitalization. Examples: Premio Nadal, El Angel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations and glosses formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: A translation following a word, phrase, or title from another language is enclosed in parentheses or quotation marks; if a non-English word other than a proper noun is presented as a parenthetical gloss, it should be in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published translations are capitalized headline-style and set in italics or quotes according to type; unpublished translations are capitalized sentence-style and not italicized. Examples: Compendio de i secreti rationali (Compendium of rational secrets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization and punctuation of foreign-language titles in English context
rubrics_metrics.description: For titles from other languages, capitalize only the words that would be capitalized in normal prose in the original language (sentence-style); punctuation may be adjusted (e.g., period to colon) and guillemets may be changed to regular quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italic vs roman for titles follows the usual rules for type of work (books in italic, short works in roman). See 8.156–201 and language-specific exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations from other languages: typographic and translation decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from a language other than English incorporated into an English text are normally treated like English quotations (set in roman and run in or block set); punctuation follows the original but may be adapted for surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation marks can usually replace guillemets; dialogue dashes should be retained in block quotations; decide whether to provide a translation based on intended audience—classicists may accept originals; general readerships should have translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source and translation placement and crediting
rubrics_metrics.description: When both a source and a translation are required in text, the source may be placed in parentheses, with the original (or translation) following, separated by a semicolon; when quoting translations, credit the translator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a published English translation, give bibliographic credit; if using author’s translations, indicate 'my translation' or name the translator. If modifying a published translation, add 'translation modified' and indicate modifications with square brackets; use such devices sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never retranslate from a secondary-language translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Never retranslate a passage from a work originally published in English (or any language) from a version that has been translated into another language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original cannot be located, paraphrase rather than retranslate. Track down the original source whenever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing translated quotations: permissible changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from published translations can be modified only with respect to the permissible changes described elsewhere; new translations provided by the author may be adjusted for consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow rules for altering quoted material (see 13.7 and related sections); indicate substantive modifications as required (e.g., 'translation modified').

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-division (hyphenation) rules for non-English languages
rubrics_metrics.description: General hyphenation rules apply to non-English languages: (1) single-syllable words should never be broken; (2) no words should be broken after one letter nor should a single letter be carried over; (3) hyphenated words and solid compounds should be broken at the hyphen or between elements if at all possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language-specific rules may differ—see the sections for particular languages. See 7.37–40 for related rules and 7.42 for proper nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include special characters and Unicode identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, phrases, or titles from another language must include any special characters that appear in the original language; authors should supply a list of special characters used within a manuscript with Unicode numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 11.1 lists special characters with Unicode numbers for Latin-alphabet languages; supply forms like 'D with stroke [U+0110]'. Ensure font/encoding compatibility across systems (see Unicode discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Phonetic symbols using IPA notation are based on the Latin alphabet and are defined in Unicode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the International Phonetic Association for the latest IPA; authors may consult phonetic reference works (bibliog.). Ensure Unicode support for IPA symbols in manuscripts.
